content: Healthcare policymakers and decision-makers often seek expert guidance on the role of insulin analogues, which are heavily promoted by pharmaceutical companies. In some countries, the expenditure on insulin analogues has exceeded the total budget allocated for insulin, resulting in shortages for certain diabetic populations who require it. A study conducted across 35 developing countries revealed that individuals with diabetes face a significantly higher risk of catastrophic personal medical expenses compared to their non-diabetic counterparts. The guidelines aim to provide public health recommendations on pharmacological agents for managing blood glucose levels in type 1 and type 2 diabetes, specifically for use in primary healthcare settings with limited resources. These recommendations are directed at the general adult, non-pregnant diabetic population. The guidelines update the World Health Organization (WHO) Package of Essential Noncommunicable Disease Interventions (PEN) recommendations regarding secondand third-line treatments for type 2 diabetes, based on evidence reviews of three newer oral hypoglycemic agents: dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, sodium-glucose co-transporter type 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors, and thiazolidinediones (TZDs), as well as insulin analogues. The newer oral medications have not demonstrated superior glycemic control compared to metformin and sulfonylureas as first-line treatments. Consequently, they have not been included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines nor recommended as first-line treatment options in evidence-based guidelines from high-income countries. However, these agents may be appropriate for intensifying treatment when metformin and/or sulfonylureas fail to achieve adequate glycemic control. Historically, before the advent of these newer agents, insulin was the primary option for such cases. The guidelines also provide updated recommendations on selecting the type of insulin (human insulin versus insulin analogues) for use in primary healthcare settings in lowand middle-income countries. The long-acting insulin analogues considered include detemir and glargine, while the short-acting analogues include aspart, lispro, and glulisine. The guidelines do not address newer formulations such as 100U and 200U insulin degludec or 300U insulin glargine due to a lack of direct comparisons with neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin. These guidelines serve as a foundation for countries to develop their own national protocols for diabetes management, focusing on blood glucose control. They are not intended to update all aspects of the WHO PEN recommendations for diabetes management, as the scope is limited to glycemic control agents. This focus reflects the dynamic nature of this field, which has seen significant changes in evidence and practice in recent years compared to other aspects of diabetes care, such as blood pressure and lipid control or the management of complications. The objectives of these guidelines include evaluating the use of DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT-2 inhibitors, and TZDs as secondand third-line treatments after metformin and sulfonylureas for managing hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes. They also aim to assess whether these oral agents are preferable to insulin in such scenarios. Additionally, the guidelines provide recommendations on the use of insulin analogues for both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The target audience for these guidelines includes policymakers, national diabetes program managers, procurement officers, clinicians, and healthcare professionals responsible for developing local treatment protocols for diabetes in primary care settings with limited resources. The recommendations are also relevant for decision-making at secondary and tertiary healthcare levels, particularly in the absence of national protocols. Other potential users include institutions involved in the education of healthcare workers, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and relief agencies to guide resource allocation. The development of these guidelines involved three groups: an internal WHO Guideline Steering Group to coordinate the process, a Guideline Development Group (comprising diabetes physicians, endocrinologists, researchers, program managers, and patient representatives), and an External Peer Review Group (including technical experts, patient group representatives, and health ministry officials from low-resource countries). The process included systematic reviews of evidence, quality assessments using tools like AMSTAR, and the application of the GRADE methodology to evaluate the quality of evidence and formulate recommendations. The recommendations were categorized as either strong or conditional, based on the confidence in the balance of desirable and undesirable effects. Strong recommendations indicate high confidence that the benefits outweigh the risks, while conditional recommendations reflect some uncertainty in this balance. The guideline development process emphasized achieving unanimous consensus among the group members, with voting as a fallback mechanism in case of disagreement. The guidelines were financially supported by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the WHO. They provide specific recommendations for oral hypoglycemic agents as secondand third-line treatments in type 2 diabetes, insulin use in type 2 diabetes when indicated, and insulin use in type 1 diabetes. For second-line treatment in type 2 diabetes, sulfonylureas are recommended for patients who do not achieve glycemic control with metformin alone or who have contraindications to metformin. However, glibenclamide should be avoided in patients aged 60 years and older due to the risk of hypoglycemia. Alternative sulfonylureas, such as gliclazide, are preferred for patients at higher risk of hypoglycemia.
